catalog_quote: Most conspicuous among the many developments which characterize Northern Paman reflection of Proto Paman is the reduction of Initial syllables (*CV1) by loss of initial consonants (*C1) and loss o[r] other reduction of immediately following vowels (*V1). Associated with initial reduction, and at least partially responsible for it is a shift of primary stress (a strictly phonetic feature) from the initial to the second syllable (*CV2) in [p. 168] Paman stems. In all Northern Paman languages, except Uradhi and its sister dialects, *C1 was lost invariably. Even in Uradhi the prevailing tendency has been toward initial loss, although *C1 is sometimes positively reflected in that language. Short *V1 was lost in some languages, retained in others, and metathesized in still others. Long *V1 was shortened in all.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Group-level, historical statement for the 13 Northern Paman varieties Hale sampled in 1960 (Aritinngithigh explicitly among them): primary stress moved from the etymological first syllable to the etymological second syllable, i.e. (after loss of the initial consonant and first vowel) onto the first vowel that follows a consonant in the modern word. Hale states the synchronic version of this rule ('the first vowel which is preceded by a consonant is stressed') only for Linngithigh (p. 179); the lending-only Languages of Cape York volume (Hale 1976b, snippet) generalises it as 'a rule which is apparently shared by all of the Northern Paman languages.. stress the first post-consonantal vowel in the word'. No Aritinngithigh-specific stress sentence exists in any source opened.
new_statements.exceptions: Uradhi and its sister dialects retain *C1 sometimes (irrelevant to Aritinngithigh, which lost *C1 invariably). Hale notes the shift is 'a strictly phonetic feature'.
new_statements.domain_note: Stems/words in citation; historical statement about Proto-Paman stems, not a synchronic word-stress description of Aritinngithigh; confidence for this particular language is low because the statement is subgroup-wide.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog arit1239 Arritinngithigh = ISO rrt = AIATSIS Y34 (Arraythinngith) = Hale 1966 'Aritinngitiy' (Linngithigh exonym; Ntrwa'ngayt name /aritinngayt/) = McConnel's Aritingiti, Sharp's Aditinngeti, Capell's Aratiniti; Sutton & Hale 2021 entry L12 Arrithinngithigh, spoken around the head of the Hey River. Distinct from Adithinngithigh (AIATSIS Y229) per Sutton 2001:459. Hale 1976a mentions at least one Aritinngithigh dialect heavily influenced by Linngithigh; Wikipedia/AUSTLANG also list Latamngit/Ladamngid (Y30) as another dialect. The quoted statement is subgroup-wide (Northern Paman), not specific to this variety.

Associated with initial reduction, and at least partially responsible for it, is a shift of primary stress (a strictly phonetic feature) from the initial to the second syllable (*CV2) in Paman stems.' -- verbatim, with the 1/2 printed as subscripts. The next paragraph on…
new_statements.relation_note: The stress sentence is verbatim the same statement that the existing_statements entry cites from Hale 1966 (AL 8-2, pp. 167-168), so this is the earlier publication of that identical group-level claim, not an independent source; it adds nothing new for Aritinngithigh specifically. It agrees with the existing reading 'fixed: other position' (stress on the etymological second = post-reduction first syllable; non-contrastive). Against the catalog record itself (classification segmental, empty rule) it supplies the only stress statement available: a diachronic Northern Paman stress shift, not a synchronic description of Aritinngithigh.
new_statements.rule_in_words: A diachronic, group-level statement for all of Northern Paman (Aritinngithigh is subgroup G of the 13 samples): primary stress, which Hale calls 'a strictly phonetic feature' (i.e. non-contrastive), shifted in Paman stems from the initial to the second syllable, and this shift drove the loss of the initial consonant and reduction of the first vowel. For the modern language this means the stressed syllable is the etymological second syllable, which after initial reduction is the first (post-consonantal) syllable of the reduced stem. Hale gives no synchronic stress rule for Aritinngithigh itself; the only Aritinngithigh-specific material is the location (head of the Hey River, p. 254), the *u metathesis examples *puŋku > ŋkwu 'knee', *yuku > kwu 'tree' (p. 260), and cognate counts (pp. 262-263).
new_statements.exceptions: none about stress; on the reduction itself: in Uradhi *C₁ is 'sometimes positively reflected' and short *V₁ 'was neither lost nor metathesized' (pp. 256, 260), so Uradhi departs from the pan-Northern-Paman pattern; Aritinngithigh is not named as an exception
new_statements.identity_note: Hale 1964 treats 'Aritiŋitiy' (also /aritiŋayt/ in Ntrwa'ŋayt) as the language originally spoken around the head of the Hey River, subgroup (G) of Northern Paman, identified with McConnel's Aritingiti, Sharp's Aditinngeti and Capell's Aratiniti (p. 254); this is the same entity as Glottolog arit1239. The stress statement is made for Northern Paman as a whole (13 samples from Weipa and Aurukun informants, 1960), not for this language separately.
